items.snippet_en: Mayo Clinic News Network stated that assertions about microchips in COVID-19 vaccines are false, and there is no way for the vaccine to track people or gather personal information. This myth originated from Bill Gates' comments about a digital certificate of vaccine records, not a microchip.

Mayo Clinic clarified that COVID-19 vaccines are made only with ingredients that help the body recognize and clear out the virus, and it is a myth that they contain microchips to track location or movement.

FactCheck.org reported that a video falsely claiming COVID-19 vaccine vials have a microchip to track patients misrepresented an interview about a chip attached to a plastic vial to store information about the vaccine dose, not to track people.

KSAT reported that local medical experts in San Antonio warned about the prevalence of misinformation, including the unfounded social media theory that COVID-19 vaccines contain microchips and tracking devices, which they determined to be untrue.
AFP Fact Check stated that social media posts claiming COVID-19 vaccines contain trackers are false, and health authorities confirm no chip is in any vaccine product.
Jala Hoaks Jakarta clarified that claims of COVID-19 vaccines containing chips to track people are false, explaining that barcodes on vaccine products are for tracking distribution, not individuals.
